title: diffuse / profuse / profound
core: Three words that look almost interchangeable on the page and all suggest, vaguely, "a lot of something." Two of them come from *fundere*, to pour, and describe how something is distributed — thinly across a space, or in a torrent out of a source. The third only looks like a pouring word: it comes from *fundus*, bottom, and measures depth rather than amount. The GRE's trap is that all three attach comfortably to the same abstract nouns — apologies, silence, changes, prose — while saying completely different things about them.

words.nuance: The only one of the three that means **less in any one place**: the quantity is unchanged, the concentration is lost. It spreads *apart* — light through frosted glass, authority across a committee. As criticism of writing it faults the structure, never the supply of material, so it sits opposite *concise* and *pointed*, not opposite *empty*.

Spreads *out of a source*, not across a space — high volume, low control, pouring faster than anyone wanted. It attaches to things that literally stream (sweat, blood, tears) and to social gestures performed past the point of comfort (**profuse** apologies, thanks, praise). It rates quantity and rate only; it says nothing about depth or sincerity, which is exactly why profuse thanks can be hollow.

Not a pouring word at all — the axis is vertical. It carries no idea of spread, volume, or excess, so nothing is ever *too* **profound** the way thanks can be too profuse. Two jobs: praise for insight that reaches bedrock, and flat description of something reaching all the way down with no compliment attached — profound deafness, profound ignorance.

exam_note: Watch the collocation swap: *profuse apologies* (too many) vs *profound regret* (deeply felt) vs a *diffuse* apology (rambling) — the exam counts on the shared -f- spelling to make you pick by sound instead of by axis: thinned-out, poured-out, or deep.
